item.title: Reserve is seeing traction on the stablecoin layer
item.dc:creator: Nevin Freeman
item.content:encoded:
By Nevin Freeman and Gabo Jimenez

Over the last 24 months, UGLYCASH has proven the model of fintechs monetizing their user balances at the DeFi rate. User balances can remain in eUSD while underlying collateral yield is directed to the fintech, simplifying the UX for the customer and the business. In today’s update, we’ll share more about the growth in this model and how we plan to take it to the next level.

Our first net-positive quarter

In Q3 2026, the Reserve ecosystem earned $139.6K in positive net revenue, a 59% net margin.

Net revenue is all the revenue that comes in across every DTF minus what we pay out to generate it, i.e. the yield paid to holders, payments to external partners, DTF incentives, and the extra eUSD yield UGLYCASH tops up for its users. Here’s how Q3 broke down:

  • Total Q3 revenue across all DTFs: $529.8K
  • Paid to holders (yield and revenue share): −$293.7K
  • Gross revenue kept by the protocol: $236.1K
  • Payments to external partners: −$25.8K
  • Resulting revenue to RSR (rewards and token burns): $210.3K
  • DTF incentives: $0
  • Extra eUSD rewards in UGLYCASH: −$70.7K
  • Net revenue to RSR ecosystem overall: +$139.6K

Reserve has had big revenue numbers before. The problem was that incentives were always bigger, so the ecosystem as a whole was losing money. Over the past year we’ve added a lot of discipline, cutting incentives quarter after quarter until revenue exceeded costs:

Two experiments, one pulling ahead

For the past couple of years, Reserve has effectively run two big experiments in parallel.

The first is UGLYCASH, the Reserve app. It’s our own consumer app, where people hold their money in eUSD.

The second is index DTFs. Onchain baskets that let anyone hold a whole investment portfolio as a single token, distributed across DeFi and other platforms.

Until recently it wasn’t clear which one would get more traction.

UGLYCASH launched its full product suite in October 2024. In the 24 months since, it has gone from zero revenue to a $5.8M annualized revenue run rate. It’s growing faster than anything else in the Reserve ecosystem.

And it’s where eUSD’s real adoption comes from. eUSD was Reserve’s biggest DTF in Q3, and about $18M of it is held by UGLYCASH users. These are real people choosing to keep their money in it, not treasury seed capital or incentive-chasing liquidity.

For a while now, it’s been a bit of a secret that eUSD has grown so much within UGLYCASH since DeFi yield farming pools in eUSD have shrunk at a similar rate, leading to a flat total eUSD supply:

As you can see in this chart, UGLYCASH users are the main holders of eUSD now, and they continue to hold more and more. eUSD adoption in UGLYCASH is growing because UGLYCASH is growing and because UGLYCASH users are putting more and more of their money into eUSD.

The fintech opportunity

We see two complementary opportunities here:

  1. We can keep growing UGLYCASH and eUSD and directly grow ecosystem revenue for RSR.
  2. We can build out a suite of revenue-generating USD products to allow fintechs to monetize idle stablecoin balances, thus offering the infrastructure layer for a better version of money.

We’re deep in the weeds as a fintech team running UGLYCASH, so we know exactly what stablecoin-based fintechs need from a user, regulatory, financial, and practical perspective.

Because eUSD’s revenue is generated from blue chip DeFi lending protocols and not by a centralized stablecoin issuer, our understanding is that eUSD is not a “Payment Stablecoin” under the GENIUS act and there is no restriction on the yield its collateral generates being paid out to stablecoin holders in the United States.

User balances can remain in eUSD while underlying collateral yield is directed to the fintech, simplifying the UX for the customer and the business.

Stablecoin-based fintech is a growing category, and we think we may have the right formula worked out to help a whole class of fintechs monetize their customer balances at the DeFi rate and offer their customers attractive rewards.

To better serve UGLYCASH and outside fintech platforms, we’re planning to build out this product line further based on everything we’ve learned.

What might that look like? We’re in the middle of work on this, and considering things like:

  • Platform fees that burn RSR as each of these assets grow
  • Separating yield and overcollateralization layers so that fintechs and their users can pick which risk and return level suits them
  • Partnership approaches that would put us on good terms with payment stablecoin issuers

We’ll share more about this next-generation revenue-generating USD product line soon.

Why UGLYCASH is working

There’s an entire generation that earns its income on the internet: freelancers, remote workers, content creators. It’s a massive global economy that barely existed ten years ago. In Latin America alone, these internet earners already move as much money as the region’s entire remittance market, and unlike remittances, it keeps growing every year.

But banks weren’t built for them. Banks were built for traditional employment in local economies. So internet earners get labeled “informal,” even though many of them out-earn people with local jobs. Getting paid, moving money and getting access to credit is slow and expensive. They lose $10 to $50 every time they get paid, wait days before they can touch their money, and often can’t get a credit card or loan at all.

That’s the problem UGLYCASH solves. Getting paid takes minutes, not days, and costs $2, not $30. Their balance sits in eUSD automatically. They can earn rewards, withdraw to a local bank, spend with the UGLYCASH Visa card, invest, and get credit built for how they actually earn.

The response has been incredibly encouraging, with growth coming from all across Latin America:

  • Active internet earners grew 33.7% in the last 90 days, in the first quarter we focused squarely on them.
  • About one in three of them now use UGLYCASH as their main account.
  • Revenue and margins rose even as we started charging more for the product, and customers stayed.

And the yield generated by eUSD’s underlying collateral is a powerful engine that makes this work economically:

  • Some users are on UGLYCASH for the transactional features and don’t claim the rewards they’re offered on their balances. For those customers, the yield their eUSD’s collateral generates offers more net revenue to the business.
  • Others use it as a savings tool and the rewards are a key reason they stay. UGLYCASH is able to offer attractive rewards due in part to its revenue share with eUSD.

You can now track eUSD usage and growth within UGLYCASH right on http://app.reserve.org:

The next 18 months: better money

For the next 18 months, Reserve will increase its focus on growing UGLYCASH and building out this suite of revenue-generating USD products for fintechs.

In addition to these new products, we’ll continue our R&D process in the direction of building other forms of better money. Conversations in the SF office over the past two weeks also included how to design an inflation-proof flatcoin given everything we’ve learned so far in DeFi and what a fully agentically-managed financial experience might look like in the near future. On the team we call this corner of the work we’re doing the “better money lab.”

But we’re deliberately not putting the spotlight on these forward-looking R&D projects. We want existing Reserve community members and newcomers to focus foremost on the exciting growth we already see in eUSD and UGLYCASH as we work on turning that trajectory exponential, and we’ll bring the more speculative parts into focus if and when they prove themselves to be promising.

Index DTFs

We’ll keep supporting index DTFs on the platform, including the community-run DTFs and the AI thematic DTFs, which we’re also integrating into UGLYCASH.

We still believe DTFs will eventually be a hugely popular way to hold capital. But based on our results so far and the regulatory challenges we still see for tokenized equities, we think we’re still early.

We’ll keep watching the market for signs of real traction. If we see them, we’ll put more energy behind whatever is catching on. Reserve’s index infrastructure is, as far as we can tell, the most developed in the space, so we can move fast when the moment comes.

Consolidating the team and tuning the leadership

To focus on this theme, we’re unifying the three teams behind Reserve (ABC Labs, Best Friend Finance and Confusion Capital) into a single operating unit.

Nevin and Gabo have been the central cofounders of Reserve. Up until now, Nevin has been the pilot and Gabo has ridden shotgun as copilot. Gabo led the founding and building of the Reserve app (originally RPay, now UGLYCASH), most recently achieving the 24 months of growth in users, revenue and eUSD balances highlighted above. Given that we’re only increasing our focus on this direction, we think it makes sense to have a lot more Gabo in the leadership position. So we’re reversing the roles: Gabo is taking the pilot’s seat, and Nevin is becoming copilot.

Same plane. Same mission. Different roles in the cockpit.

A leaner, fintech-oriented team

As part of this change, we’ve reduced the size of the ABC Labs team, eliminating roles that aren’t directly tied to the near-term plan. That was a hard decision. We chose to say goodbye to many talented, passionate, smart, fun and inspirational people who helped build what Reserve is today, and we’re grateful to every one of them.

It wasn’t a decision about money running out. At our previous spending rate, we already had more than four years of runway. But there is a financial benefit to the ecosystem: with this new setup, we aim to operate entirely on the return the treasury earns each year. That gives Reserve an effectively infinite runway, and it means we shouldn’t need to sell RSR to fund operations, unless we hit a moment where it’s worth spending more to speed up the flywheel.

Connecting UGLYCASH and RSR

UGLYCASH is run by its own company, Best Friend Finance (BFF). BFF was started as a wholly-owned subsidiary of Confusion Capital, and has recently started offering equity incentives to some of its employees.

One of the questions we hear most often is a fair one: if UGLYCASH grows, do RSR holders actually benefit, or does the value stay with the company?

We’ve worked hard to make sure the answer doesn’t depend on anyone’s good intentions. We’ve set up the contracts and financial incentives so that UGLYCASH succeeding in a big way brings massive growth to Reserve and value to RSR. Here’s how that will work, beginning with what’s already in place.

Already in place:

  • Every UGLYCASH balance is eUSD. Users’ balances sit in eUSD automatically. eUSD’s collateral earns yield, and a share of that yield goes to the RSR stakers who protect eUSD. As UGLYCASH grows, eUSD grows, and so do the revenue to RSR stakers and the amount of RSR that needs to be staked. If we update the way our revenue-generating USD assets work, we’ll ensure value continues to flow to the Reserve ecosystem.
  • UGLYCASH is contractually bound to Reserve assets. BFF has a legal agreement with Confusion Capital, the steward of the Reserve treasury. BFF receives some RSR to help fund UGLYCASH’s growth. In exchange, at least 50% of the assets users hold on UGLYCASH must be Reserve assets: tokens that run on the Reserve protocols. The contractual commitment lasts 100 years. UGLYCASH can only go below 50% if Confusion Capital agrees that doing so is still the best thing for Reserve.
  • The founders only win big if UGLYCASH grows Reserve. About half (48.3%) of the BFF equity that UGLYCASH’s leaders can earn (Gabo, Josh Furnas and BFF’s CTO Matt Robinson) only vests if UGLYCASH keeps meeting that 50% threshold. This isn’t a small bonus; it’s half of their potential equity. The three people with the most control over UGLYCASH’s strategy are personally, financially tied to Reserve’s growth.
  • If UGLYCASH is sold in the near term, the value still comes back to Reserve. For its funding of UGLYCASH, Confusion Capital has a seed investor share of equity. In addition, if UGLYCASH were ever sold off because it wasn’t working out, the founders’ performance-based equity would never have vested. It would stay with Confusion Capital too, so the proceeds would flow back to the Reserve treasury and hence the Reserve ecosystem instead of to the founders.

New this quarter:

  • Team RSR only unlocks when RSR is up. Team members still earn part of their compensation in RSR. Starting this quarter, new and renegotiated RSR grants (typically two years long) only unlock after RSR trades above 1¢ for three months straight (measured with its two-week moving average), which hasn’t happened since 2021–22. Each later round of grants will have a new price target, which will be higher if we are starting at a price above 1¢. Team members who finish their time with Reserve keep their earned (but still illiquid) RSR and can still benefit if the target is hit later. So the team can’t cash out unless the market supports it, and paying the team in RSR doesn’t add selling pressure at today’s prices.
  • One team, one plan: With Gabo leading both UGLYCASH and the Reserve protocol development and deployment, there’s no longer one set of priorities for the app and another for the protocol and its stakers.

Being explored: a direct link to UGLYCASH’s value in an IPO

Today, the link between UGLYCASH’s equity value and RSR holders runs through Confusion Capital as the steward of the Reserve treasury. That works, but it depends on trusting Confusion Capital to keep reinvesting in Reserve, and it’s a complicated story to explain.

We want something simpler and more direct. We’re exploring ways for RSR holders to participate directly in UGLYCASH’s value if it’s ever sold or goes public, instead of that value only reaching them through the Reserve treasury. “If UGLYCASH goes public, part of the value goes to RSR holders” is a story anyone can understand.

We don’t know yet whether we can do this. It has to work without complicating RSR’s legal status, which we won’t put at risk to get there. We’ll share more once we have something concrete.

But even before this final step: UGLYCASH can’t grow without growing eUSD, and its founders can’t win big unless UGLYCASH acts as a vehicle for Reserve’s growth.

The race ahead

No one is saying this next phase will be easy. We’re in the middle of a gold rush, with fintechs across the world growing and competing, agentic finance rolling out across platforms, and revenue-sharing top of mind for many. Plenty of companies and crypto projects are throwing money at this market. But we’re in the running for that race so far: UGLYCASH is already among the top fintechs serving internet earners in Latin America, and we intend to keep that lead, along with marketing our revenue-sharing USD products across platforms.

It’s exciting to have found a direction that’s working financially, providing real value and serving a growing number of users. Now it’s time to take it further than ever before.

Nevin & Gabo

item.title: AI Supercycle Weekly — Sep 9, 2026
item.dc:creator: Jake “starl3xx” Bouma
item.content:encoded:
The week the frontier labs upped their game

Okay we can conclusively put to rest the idea that open model advances would somehow deter frontier lab appetite for SOTA model development. In a single week, we had major model releases from Anthropic and OpenAI, with a leader of the latter calling their release the start of the AGI era. Sound like hyperbole? Well: Astra did break new ground by having the capability to drive a computer the same way a human would, representing an innovation. Plus, the whole Navier-Stokes thing, from a model they haven’t even shipped. In the same way that the agentic revolution was the spark for the AI supercycle, these new developments will represent the next escalation of the AI buildout, which based on last week’s earnings remains in full swing.

The supply chain continues to accelerate but expectations remain high

  • AI stalwarts continue to post massive increases to their forecasts. Broadcom guided AI revenues towards doubling both next year AND the year after, with major labs like Anthropic planning for 5 GW worth of Broadcom chips alone. Dell posted its largest ever quarter of AI servers and now sits on a record backlog of $95B, with management specifically highlighting inference overtaking training as the bigger workload.
  • Memory remains the biggest bottleneck. With the majority of producer volume now locked up through LTAs and prices continuing to surge, Nvidia has been forced to cut memory on Rubin Ultra from 12-high to 8-high stacks as it now represents 40% of the total capital cost of ownership.
  • Earnings beats are everywhere but expectations are also high. Credo and Ciena both posted banner quarters but saw major drops in share price. This further reinforces our view that markets have aggressively pre-priced much of the demand pull from the agent revolution, and the next innovation is required for a meaningful upward revision of expectations.
  • The risk of power and basic raw materials such as steel becoming major constraints to the buildout continues to rise. Musk specifically called out the possibility of some 15 GW of compute that cannot be turned on, where the chips are delivered without the necessary racks to house them nor the electricity to actually power them.

Additional thoughts over the Labor Day weekend

As the wealth creation effects from the AI revolution proliferate through the economy, the dichotomy between the wealthy and ordinary people continues to widen at an alarming rate (the so-called K-shaped economy). Inflation remains persistent and sticky, with most Americans dealing with high energy costs and an uncertain job market that is being disrupted by AI. Meanwhile, sales of luxury cars and collectibles continue to hit all-time highs as most of the wealth created by AI accrues to the upper echelons of society. As AI further advances and proliferates from highly capable agents to general robotics, the impact of this disruption will only widen as a broader spectrum of physical and skilled labor becomes subject to displacement. If an increasingly larger share of people fail to share in the productivity gains of AI while mega datacenters are erected in their backyard, then we risk veering into some very dystopian and potentially violent outcomes. The current and coming administrations will have the unique task of not only taming inflation, but ensuring some equitable distribution of the value created by AI in order to maintain social order.

The week ahead

  • Wed 9/9: Apple’s iPhone event. New CEO John Ternus’s first launch, with a foldable iPhone the leading rumor. Apple has a quiet AI angle too: labs are buying its Macs by the thousands for training work.
  • Thu 9/10: Oracle and Adobe report after the close. Oracle is the best read on how much AI data-center capacity is being leased and at what price. Adobe tests whether AI is helping or eating software companies.
  • On the horizon: the ECOC optical-networking conference in Europe (Sept 20–24) is where next-generation chip-to-chip optics gets unveiled; Micron reports in late September; Anthropic’s IPO filing could land any time after that.

item.title: AI Supercycle Weekly — Aug 17, 2026
item.dc:creator: Jake “starl3xx” Bouma
item.content:encoded:
A toll road made of chips

The biggest development in AI last week wasn’t a new chip or model breakthrough, it was a financing structure. On Monday, Nvidia announced agreements with Apollo, BlackRock, Blackstone, Brookfield, Goldman Sachs and KKR, six of the largest pools of private capital on earth, to build platforms aimed at mobilizing more than $500 billion for AI infrastructure. Under this proposed structure, financing flows to independent platforms that sit off Nvidia’s balance sheet and pays for data centers built with Nvidia hardware.

That’s a significant departure from how data centers are currently funded.

Until now, data centers were funded the boring way: hyperscalers spent profits to build, and borrowed on their balance sheets when the needs exceeded near term cash flows. Nvidia’s proposal gives a warehouse full of GPUs the same economic life and productivity as a toll road, opening the gates for off-balance sheet non-recourse financing of the sort commonly found in steady cash flowing infrastructure assets. With some of the world’s largest private asset allocators signaling their willingness to play ball, this announcement very likely represents the next escalation point in the AI buildout.

For the above to go right, many things still must happen. First, actual deals need to emerge from the agreement for it to have teeth. Second, long-term viability of the structure requires validation that a five-year-old chip can remain an economically productive asset and qualify as collateral. Lastly, for the AI buildout to happen, datacenters need to be approved and be built on time. That’s no longer a given, with rising local resistance and local power grids straining under the potential demand pull. These problems will only worsen as we progress, especially as AI’s impact on the economy and society becomes even more profound.

Builders of compute are unlikely to be dissuaded given the magnitude of rewards. The most recent round of earnings continued to affirm that demand is not the problem, with Applied Materials posting blowout earnings and SanDisk providing an extremely rosy multi-year forecast during its investor day. One company’s gains are now coming at the cost of another’s margins. Cisco was notably punished during earnings last week as it missed margins due to higher memory costs.

Further upstream, the chokepoint got tighter. Coherent told investors it won’t sell its indium phosphide lasers, the light sources that move data between chips, to outside customers for the foreseeable future. That’s the corporate way of saying ours now, and it shrinks an already tiny open market to a handful of suppliers. It lands just as Nvidia reportedly shifts its 2027 systems away from memory and toward optics. And Samsung has started using Anthropic’s Claude Code for chip design, reportedly compressing a month of work into two days.

Baidu reports Tuesday and Alibaba Thursday, both useful reads on Chinese AI demand. Then everything defers to Nvidia on August 26, still the one print that resets the entire sector, and now the referee in the memory-versus-optics fight.

item.title: AI Supercycle Weekly — Aug 10, 2026
item.dc:creator: Jake “starl3xx” Bouma
item.content:encoded:
Dispersion returns

Friday’s weaker-than-expected jobs report threw cold water on the prospects of a September rate hike, and the markets responded accordingly: the S&P closed at a record, up 3.6% on the week. Underneath that, though, AI was a tale of two worlds. Market participants heavily favored photonics over memory, the prior darlings, and the resulting gap in performance was wide enough to be the story of the week rather than a footnote to it.

The genesis of that performance came from industry reports pointing to NVIDIA’s decision to reduce HBM content in Rubin Ultra — high-bandwidth memory, the expensive stuff stacked beside the processor — because the memory shortage is now severe enough to constrain how many racks get built at all. What NVIDIA gives up there it takes back by increasing the photonic content, moving data between chips faster rather than holding more of it close by. A straightforward engineering trade-off. It is also the first major signal that the AI trade has entered its next, more nuanced stage.

The magnitude of semiconductor component scarcity across the entire supply chain is now so extensive that OEMs must make short-term trade-offs. NVIDIA’s is simply the first to become visible, and it will not be the last. Each one will move money from one vertical to another on a timescale that has nothing to do with underlying demand. The same pressure is everywhere you look: lasers sold out two years deep, three companies on earth growing the crystal those lasers are made from, TSMC reportedly sitting on a billion dollars of finished Apple processors it cannot package because it cannot get memory. When everything is short at once, sacrifices inevitably have to be made somewhere.

So where do we go from here? The long-term trajectory for almost every participant in the AI buildout is still up. But the uniform, up-only price action we saw earlier in the year will likely be rarer, with most names now seeing periods of meaningful over- and under-performance. Coming into this year, owning the next incremental narrative bottleneck was generally enough to capture massive gains in a short period of time despite what the underlying fundamentals suggested. With market participants now much better informed, capturing the next leg of gains will require a mix of careful selection and patience.

The week ahead

  • Mon 8/10: Rocket Lab and AST SpaceMobile. Space trades as AI infrastructure now, on increasingly serious talk of data centers in orbit.
  • Tue 8/11: Lumentum and CoreWeave. The first real test of whether the recent bounce in optics can have further legs.
  • Wed 8/12: July inflation, plus NBIS and COHR. The deciding input for September now that the jobs number took the hawks’ best argument away.
  • Thu 8/13: SanDisk’s investor day. Flash has noticeably lagged the rest of the memory complex, and this will be the first major opportunity for management to reignite investor excitement by providing details on their new flash-memory standard.

item.title: The entire AI supply chain is now tradable onchain
item.dc:creator: Jake “starl3xx” Bouma
item.content:encoded:
Hello, 你好, 안녕하세요, नमस्ते, مرحبا, Hola, Bonjour.

Have you figured out how to own your share of the AI industry yet?
你想好如何拥有属于你的那份人工智能产业了吗？
AI 산업에서 당신의 몫을 소유하는 방법을 이미 알아내셨나요?
क्या आपने यह पता लगा लिया है कि AI उद्योग में अपना हिस्सा कैसे हासिल करें?
هل اكتشفت بعد كيف تمتلك حصتك في صناعة الذكاء الاصطناعي؟
¿Ya has descubierto cómo poseer tu parte de la industria de la inteligencia artificial?
Avez-vous déjà trouvé comment posséder votre part de l’industrie de l’IA?

We’ve all seen the incredible appreciation of companies participating in the AI buildout. But we haven’t all been able to invest.

Some of us had trouble getting a brokerage account with access to US equities. Others just didn’t have the time to research hundreds of companies and figure out which ones were relevant.

We decided to knock down those barriers.

Reserve has turned the AI supply chain trade into five decentralized token funds, each for a unique layer of the supply chain:

  • $BUILDOUT — AI infrastructure overall: the whole stack
  • $POWER — AI power: the electricity it runs on
  • $PHOTON — AI photonics: the light layer that moves the data
  • $NEOCLOUD — AI capacity: the companies that rent compute as a service
  • $ROBOTS — Robotics: AI coming into the physical world

Each is a single, publicly investable token on BNB Chain, built from US-listed companies and held as Ondo Finance Global Markets tokenized stocks.

Because they’re onchain, we can bring them online faster than traditional finance: a US ETF takes around 75 days from registration to live trading, while an onchain fund like these can go live just a few days after the assets are tokenized — Ondo only just released most of these stocks on June 17th! And of course each of the above trades 24/7 and is redeemable onchain for the assets inside it any time.

These products are available in about 145 countries for about 6 billion people, not including the US. Why launch bundles of US stocks and exclude US buyers? Regulatory constraints don’t (yet) allow such products here — we hope to serve a US audience in the future. But the entire world is interested in owning its share of the AI revolution, so we thought it prudent to begin with this global offering as soon as possible.

This new line of DTFs covers every layer of the physical stack that’s being built out to enable the next generations of AI. Why cover physical infrastructure rather than the software companies?

AI is much, much more than a software story.

Before any model can answer a prompt, someone has to fabricate the chips, build the datacenters, generate the power, and lay the cables.

It’s one of the largest industrial buildouts in history, and a big slice of it runs through several dozen public US-traded companies, from mega-cap semiconductor producers to obscure food additives companies.

Let’s break them all down.

BUILDOUT

The context: What we call “AI” is actually a complex physical stack of chips, racks, cooling, power generation, and networking. Some people want to go deep on which layer of the stack is the next bottleneck in an attempt to frontrun the industry and get the highest return. Others just want to buy the whole stack and enjoy broad exposure. Looking at the historical backtest of this category, you can see this wouldn’t have been too bad a strategy since the start of 2026.

The numbers: World Semiconductor Trade Statistics put global semiconductor sales at roughly $796 billion in 2025, climbing to ~$1.5 trillion in 2026 in a memory-led surge as AI demand outruns supply.

All that spending flows through a concentrated set of mostly public companies: the GPU and specialized chip designers, the companies that actually fabricate the chips, the memory makers, and the equipment giants whose machines make advanced silicon possible at all.

The Reserve AI Infrastructure DTF ($BUILDOUT) is built around these companies: the 25 largest US-listed names across the AI hardware stack. One token gives you exposure to a weighted basket spanning the entire AI infrastructure stack: from AI chip designers NVIDIA ($NVDA), AMD ($AMD) and Broadcom ($AVGO), to the main factory that produces them all TSMC ($TSM) and memory maker Micron ($MU), down to the equipment makers: ASML ($ASML), Applied Materials ($AMAT), Lam Research ($LRCX), whose machines every advanced chip depends on.

You can find more info and trade $BUILDOUT on the Reserve website here: https://app.reserve.org/bsc/index-dtf/buildout/overview

POWER

The context: Where there’s smoke, there’s fire… and where there’s AI, there’s electricity. A single AI data center can draw as much power as a major city, and the grid wasn’t built for hundreds of them. Power is foundational. That’s what makes it one of the most interesting bottlenecks in the AI buildout.

The numbers: The demand curve is close to vertical. Goldman Sachs Research estimates US data-center power demand will roughly triple — from about 32 gigawatts in 2025 to somewhere around 95 gigawatts by 2030. To keep up, hyperscalers are signing power deals directly with nuclear operators and racing to bring new generation online — GE Vernova’s gas-turbine backlog alone has swelled to roughly 100 GW.

Meeting that demand takes a full stack: the companies that generate the power (gas turbines, nuclear, fuel cells), the ones that move and condition it (grid and electrical equipment), and the power chips that deliver it cleanly to the racks.

The Reserve AI Power DTF ($POWER) is built around these companies. One token gives you exposure to a weighted basket of US-listed power names behind the buildout: from gas-turbine and grid maker GE Vernova (GEV), to electrical and cooling leaders Eaton (ETN) and Vertiv (VRT), to nuclear producer Constellation (CEG) and power-chip makers like onsemi (ON).

You can find more info and trade $POWER on the Reserve website here: https://app.reserve.org/bsc/index-dtf/power/overview

PHOTON

The context: Imagine if Paul Revere could’ve just dropped “The British are coming!” in the group chat. Alas, information moves at the speed of its delivery mechanism. For decades, data inside servers moved as electricity through copper wire. But today’s AI chips are advancing so quickly that copper can’t keep up: it generates too much heat, carries too little bandwidth, and can’t reliably move data far enough. The solution is light: data centers are increasingly using optical connections to move information between chips, replacing electrons with photons. This technology, called photonics, radically increases the amount of optical hardware packed into every AI system.

The numbers: Goldman Sachs estimates spending on optical components for AI data centers will grow from $15 billion in 2026 to $154 billion by 2028, or roughly a 10x jump in two years. And the biggest player, NVIDIA, is already moving: in March 2026, they committed $2 billion each to Coherent and Lumentum, two of the largest makers of the laser chips this entire buildout runs on.

Photonics is still a young industry, and its supply chain sits in a small handful of public companies: the ones making the fiber, the lasers, the transceivers, the photonics chips, and the wafers those lasers are grown on.

The Reserve AI Photonics DTF ($PHOTON) is built around these companies. One token gives you exposure to a weighted basket of US-listed photonics names spanning the full optical supply chain: from Corning ($GLW), the company that invented low-loss optical fiber, to laser leaders Coherent ($COHR) and Lumentum ($LITE), down to the specialty chips and wafers the whole industry depends on.

You can find more info and trade $PHOTON on the Reserve website here: https://app.reserve.org/bsc/index-dtf/photon/overview

NEOCLOUD

The context: If you need somewhere to crash for a night or two, you don’t buy a hotel. Likewise, if you need AI compute, you probably don’t need to build a whole data center. Building one costs billions, so most companies that need serious compute don’t build AI data centers… they simply rent the computing power. A cottage industry has sprung up to meet that demand: “neoclouds” and power-rich data-center operators that raise the capital, secure the power, and rent out GPU compute by the hour.

The numbers: Independent researchers size the neocloud / GPU-cloud market at about $35 billion a year in 2026, growing past $180 billion a year by 2030 — roughly 5x (Mordor Intelligence puts 2026 near $35B; Synergy Research Group is cited reaching ~$180B by 2030). And the backlogs are already enormous: CoreWeave alone reports roughly $99 billion in contracted backlog, and Nebius around $50 billion from the likes of Microsoft and Meta.

The players split into two camps: the pure-play AI cloud operators, and the power-rich hosts — many of them former miners — converting energized sites into GPU and AI-data-center capacity.

The Reserve AI Capacity Neocloud DTF ($NEOCLOUD) is built around these companies. One token gives you exposure to a weighted basket of US-listed names turning capital, silicon and electricity into compute: from neocloud operators Nebius (NBIS) and CoreWeave (CRWV), to operator-host IREN (IREN), to power-rich hosts TeraWulf (WULF), Hut 8 (HUT) and Applied Digital (APLD).

You can find more info and trade $NEOCLOUD on the Reserve website here: https://app.reserve.org/bsc/index-dtf/neocloud/overview

ROBOTS

The context: You blinked, and science fiction became science fact: robots are real now. The same breakthroughs that taught software to reason are teaching machines to perceive, decide, and act, and even to take on physical labor. Robotics is where the innovations of AI transcend the chat box and become an embodied reality.

The numbers: In the bookends of a speculative forecast, Morgan Stanley estimates the humanoid-robot market could reach something like $5 trillion by 2050, with around a billion robots in service. On the other, more conservative end, Goldman Sachs puts the number at about $38 billion by 2035. Either way, capital is already following: industry trackers reported over $34 billion flowing into robotics in 2025.

And it spans far more than humanoids: we’re talking surgical robots, factory and warehouse automation, self-driving systems, and the lidar, machine-vision, and edge chips that help machines navigate the real world.

The Reserve Robotics DTF ($ROBOTS) is built around these companies. One token gives you exposure to a weighted basket of US-listed robotics and automation names: from robotic-surgery leader Intuitive Surgical ($ISRG), to factory-automation Rockwell ($ROK) and warehouse robotics Symbotic ($SYM), down to autonomy and sensor names like Mobileye ($MBLY) and Ouster ($OUST).

You can find more info and trade $ROBOTS on the Reserve website here: https://app.reserve.org/bsc/index-dtf/robots/overview

How do DTFs work under the hood?

All five DTFs live on BNB Chain. You can buy and sell them onchain at app.reserve.org and Bitget Wallet, or on DEXes like PancakeSwap X and CoW Swap — 24/7, with no minimum or maximum purchase size. A 0.3% minting fee and a 0.6% TVL fee apply. Eligibility follows Ondo’s geographic rules: it’s not available in the US or sanctioned jurisdictions, some countries require accreditation or equivalent, and elsewhere you can connect a wallet and buy. You’re responsible for following your local laws.

They’re powered by Reserve, the onchain platform for building decentralized token funds of all kinds: think the blockchain version of ETFs (though a DTF is not an ETF, and is not regulated like one). Reserve got started in 2018 with backing from Sam Altman and Peter Thiel, and has spent millions on code audits. As with any DeFi app, you use it at your own risk.

What’s the role of RSR?

Reserve, the protocol powering all five DTFs, is governed by the Reserve Rights token ($RSR), and RSR is wired directly into how the DTFs work.

  • Lock to govern. Users can lock RSR to receive vlRSR (vote-locked RSR) and help govern the DTFs: which companies qualify for a basket, how it’s weighted,etc. On BNB Chain, every DTF feeds a single vlRSR staking vault, on a 7-day governance cycle (with a 7-day unlocking delay).
  • Governors share in the fees. Each DTF charges a 0.3% mint fee and a 0.6% TVL fee. After a standard platform cut, the rest flows to vlRSR governors: it’s converted into RSR and added to your staked position automatically, with no manual claiming.
  • The monthly burn. The protocol’s cut of fees are also used to buy back and burn $RSR, fully transparent via the RSR burn dashboard on Dune.

The $RSR contract address on BNB Chain is:

0x23f72a3Db61D6CB8aBE5d9AF1Ac4B6c99327bFee

Users who wish to bridge are recommended to use Portal Bridge.

The AI buildout is happening. Own your share of it.

Follow Reserve for what’s next.

The market-size figures cited (Goldman Sachs, WSTS, ABI Research, and Morgan Stanley) are third-party estimates of market size, are inherently uncertain, and are not forecasts of any fund’s performance. ABC Labs designed each fund’s methodology and selected its initial constituents accordingly. Decentralized governance is incentivized to follow that methodology to enact quarterly rebalancing. item.title: Spring cleaning: A proposal to deprecate abandoned DTFs
item.dc:creator: Jake “starl3xx” Bouma
item.content:encoded:
ABC Labs is proposing the formal deprecation of 17 dormant DTFs, and we want to be upfront about why.

Every DTF on this list requires active attention — governance alerts, role monitoring, infrastructure overhead — regardless of whether anyone is actually using it. ABC Labs is the one carrying the ongoing administrative cost of monitoring these products. Deprecating the products that aren’t going anywhere lets us focus that attention on the ones that are.

Our goal is to reduce the surface of what we need to actively monitor, without increasing risk to anyone holding these tokens.

If you currently hold any of these tokens: redemption remains live throughout this process, including RSR unstaking. You can exit for your pro-rata share of underlying assets at any time. This proposal doesn’t change that.

  • Yield DTFs to be deprecated: dgnETH, hyUSD (mainnet), hyUSD (Base), MAAT, KNOX, USDC+, BSDX, VAYA, rgUSD
  • Index DTFs to be deprecated: mvRWA, mvDEFI, AI, VTF, CLUB, MVDA25, SBR, ZINDEX

The case for formal deprecation comes down to three things:

  1. Resource waste. Monitoring infrastructure like Hypernative costs real money and attention. Paying for it on 17 unused products is indefensible.
  2. User confusion. Abandoned funds look identical to active ones in the Reserve app. That’s a bad (and misleading) experience.
  3. Security risk. Unmonitored contracts still hold live governance roles, which amounts to unnecessary exposure with no upside.

The proposed action is to run deprecateFolio on each index (disabling issuance) and removing admin roles, then tag them as deprecated in the app. Redemption stays live throughout. Holders can exit for their pro-rata share of underlying assets at any time, nothing changes there.

The RFC is open for community feedback before it goes to a formal vote. If you hold any of the affected tokens or have a reason a specific DTF should stay active, we want to hear from you.

Read the full RFC →

item.title: Deprecating Yield DTF Batch Auctions: EasyAuction.sol Division-by-Zero
item.dc:creator: Patrick Mckelvy
item.content:encoded:
Summary

A whitehat security researcher GregoAI (@therealgregoAI) / X recently uncovered a vulnerability in the backup auction infrastructure used by Reserve Yield Protocol DTFs. The bug affected the Gnosis EasyAuction contract — a third-party, non-upgradeable contract that the Reserve Yield Protocol used as a fallback trading mechanism, and that had not been used in over two years. If exploited under very specific edge circumstances, it could have permanently locked funds that were actively inside an auction, with no recovery path. However, an attacker would merely have been able to lock funds, not extract them, which made the incentive to attack low.

The relevant trading functions in affected DTFs have already been paused prior to making this announcement, so no meaningful funds are at risk, and the process to deprecate this fallback trading mechanism is underway. The bug was never exploited, merely uncovered by a whitehat security researcher, responsibly disclosed, and addressed. This is a report to share the info for community awareness.

How Reserve Protocol Auctions Worked

When a yield DTF needs to rebalance its collateral or process revenue, it opens a trade. There are two paths for this: Dutch Auctions (the default, recommended method) and Batch Auctions via the Gnosis EasyAuction contract.

Critically, the rebalance() function is public, and anyone can choose which auction type to use. This meant an attacker would have been able to force the protocol down the Batch Auction path at will.

The Bug

The vulnerability was a division-by-zero that could be triggered during auction settlement. Here was how it worked in plain terms:

  1. Force the vulnerable path. An attacker calls rebalance() and specified Batch Auction mode, sending up to $1M (current maxTradeVolume on yield DTFs) of DTF into the EasyAuction contract.
  2. Place a tiny bid. During the auction window, the attacker places a minimal bid — as little as a fraction of a cent. In order to realize the bug, the full lot on auction CANNOT be filled. If the full lot has been bid, then the bug can not surface in step 3. This means that if other auction participants fills the bid, no funds would be at risk — only remaining inventory that was not sold.
  3. Poison the settlement state. After the auction ends, the attacker needs to call a public helper function called precalculateSellAmountSum(). This function was designed to pre-process bids to make settlement cheaper, but when called with carefully chosen parameters, it advances the auction's internal cursor to the very end of the bid list.
  4. Settlement permanently reverted. When anyone then tries to settle the auction, the settlement logic picks up where the pre-calculation left off — but there are no more bids to process. Key variables remain at zero, and the code would hit a 0 ÷ 0 operation, which causes an irreversible revert.

Because the EasyAuction contract is non-upgradeable and had no admin rescue function, this is not a temporary freeze. If exploited, the funds would be permanently locked in a contract that could never release them.

What Would Have Been at Stake

The impact is twofold:

  • Protocol collateral (up to $1M per auction) can be permanently frozen.
  • All third-party bids placed during the auction would also be frozen, since bidders can only reclaim funds after settlement (which could never complete). In a well-attended (but unfilled) auction, this could have meant losses of nearly double the maxTradeVolume of $1M.

Beyond the immediate loss, the protocol’s internal trade counter would have been stuck, blocking all future trades until governance intervened through a multi-day process.

Why This Was Serious

Several factors compounded the severity:

  • No access control: Anyone could trigger the vulnerable auction path.
  • Low cost to attack: The attacker only needed a negligible bid amount.
  • No recovery: The EasyAuction contract could not be upgraded or admin-rescued.
  • Collateral damage: Innocent bidders would have lost their deposits too.
  • Protocol disruption: All rebalancing would have halted until governance acted.

Why This Was Low Risk

There was no direct incentive to cause this bug to surface, since the funds ended up locked in the auction contract, not in the attacker’s possession.

Additionally, a critical requirement to realizing the bug was for the full lot on auction to not be filled. Batch auctions were priced in a way to incentivize bidders to make money, and bidding was fully permissionless. It is reasonable to assume that every auctioned lot would be filled.

Finally, dutch auctions are the main yield DTF auction method. Batch auctions have not been used in over 2 years. An attacker would have needed to front-run the launch of a dutch auction in order to launch a batch auction, and even then, ABC Labs could have participated in said batch auction, filling the lot and nullifying the attack.

Mitigation

While we considered the execution of this attack to be low risk, ABC Labs treated this bug with the utmost urgency and care.

  1. Every yield DTF has a Trade Pauser role that could act in times of emergency. Because there were user funds at risk while batch auctions were still enabled, ABC Labs worked to ensure trading was paused across all active yield DTFs. As of this post, trading for over >99% of TVL in yield DTFs had been paused.
  2. Governance proposals have been made to set the batchAuctionLength to 0, disabling the use of batch auctions in any form. stRSR governance takes 8 days to complete, so in just over 1 week batch auctions will be disabled, and trading will be unpaused.

NOTE: Pausing trading did not affect any other DTF functionality. Minting & redeeming are still enabled. stRSR is unable to be unstaked or withdrawn while trading is paused.

Conclusion

A bug was recently found in a 3rd party contract used by Yield DTFs. It was never exploited, the risk has been mitigated, and funds are safe.

We appreciate the hard work of the whitehat GregoAI (@therealgregoAI) / X for submitting their bug report to our Immunefi bug bounty program.

We encourage stRSR holders of any yield DTF to go vote on the pending proposals to disable batch auctions.

item.title: Peter Thiel on the Dollar’s Global Dominance
item.dc:creator: Jake “starl3xx” Bouma
item.content:encoded:
At Monetarium, our Dialogs series brings together influential thinkers to explore pressing monetary challenges. In July 2025, we hosted PayPal co-founder and Palantir chairman Peter Thiel for an intimate Washington D.C. discussion on “The Debt, the Dollar, and Our Options From Here” with 50 subject matter experts, including Confusion Capital’s Lead Macroeconomics Research Economist, Dr. Gina Pieters.

In this exchange, Dr. Pieters raises a provocative question: could the dollar maintain reserve currency status through its role as a “global unit of account” even after America loses military superpower status? She suggests this financial dominance could allow U.S. debt to continue in a “weird zombie way” because countries would still need dollars to price goods globally. This disentanglement of financial power from military power represents a “new aspect in this world.”

Thiel responds by focusing on the concrete example of oil pricing in dollars — the petrodollar system. Is this “just a unit of account” where Saudi Arabia could theoretically convert dollars immediately after each sale, or is it “unbelievably profound geopolitically”? He points to the stark example of Saddam Hussein, who switched to pricing Iraqi oil in Euros about a year before the U.S. invasion. The message was clear: the U.S. Dollar and the U.S. military are connected at a foundational level. While Thiel admits uncertainty about separating these dimensions, his intuition leans toward the dollar’s dominance being “linked to all these weird forms of American exceptionalism rather than just a silly accounting convention.”

item.title: Community Update: Where To Talk Reserve
item.dc:creator: Jake “starl3xx” Bouma
item.content:encoded:
As the Reserve community continues to grow, we’re making it easier to understand where to go for what. From now on, our Discord and Telegram channels will each serve a clear purpose. Whether you’re just discovering Reserve or already deep in the ecosystem, this guide will help you know where to plug in.

TL;DR:

  • Use Telegram for real-time conversation, community engagement, and open access.
  • Use Discord for verified holder discussions, governance, and curated updates.

This update reflects what is already happening. Most day-to-day conversation takes place on Telegram, while more focused and in-depth discussions happen on Discord. We are embracing that behavior and building around it.

What Telegram Is For

Telegram is now the main hub for open conversation about Reserve. It is fast, easy to join, and fits the style of crypto-native communities. Whether you are a new user, a casual holder, or someone curious about Decentralized Token Folios (DTFs), Telegram is where you will find active discussion.

Expect real-time chats about protocol updates, ecosystem moves, and market narratives. Telegram will also be where most onboarding and casual feedback takes place. It is open to everyone, requires no wallet connection, and will be actively supported by the team and community moderators.

What Discord Is For

Discord has been restructured into a focused space for serious participants. It is now the home for RSR holders, governance contributors, and those more deeply involved in the protocol. To improve signal quality, we have removed unused channels and simplified the layout.

The general and governance channels are now token-gated, requiring at least 100 RSR to access. Verification is handled through Guild. This small threshold helps keep spam and low-effort content out, while giving active participants the space to contribute meaningfully.

Inside Discord, you will find official announcements, key links, and governance discussions. If you are involved in protocol decisions or want to track the evolution of RTokens and DTFs closely, this is where to be. It is structured, calm, and focused on long-term engagement.

Why We Are Doing This

This update is about clarity and purpose. Telegram gives us reach, energy, and a wide entry point for new users. Discord offers focus, structure, and a space for high-context conversation.

By clearly separating the roles of each channel, we reduce noise and help everyone get more value from both platforms. Telegram keeps the door open for broad engagement. Discord creates space for governance and contribution.

This is not about dividing the community. It is about helping each part of the community thrive in the environment that best suits it.

Use Telegram if you want to hang out, ask questions, share ideas, or stay in the loop through casual conversation. Use Discord if you are holding RSR, participating in governance, or looking for structured updates and discussions.

Both channels are live, active, and important. Choose the space that matches how you want to engage. We’ll see you there.

item.title: Peter Thiel on America’s Unspoken Debt Crisis
item.dc:creator: Jake “starl3xx” Bouma
item.content:encoded:
An exclusive video clip from Monetarium Dialogs

At Monetarium, our Dialogs series brings together influential thinkers to explore pressing monetary challenges. In July 2025, we hosted PayPal co-founder and Palantir chairman Peter Thiel for an intimate Washington D.C. discussion on “The Debt, the Dollar, and Our Options From Here” with 50 subject matter experts.

In this exclusive clip, Thiel uses his classic PayPal pitch prop — a $100 bill — to explore what gives money its value. The bill states it’s “legal tender for all debts, public and private,” and Thiel reveals the violence implicit in this seemingly simple phrase. You must use dollars to pay taxes; if you don’t pay, “some people will come after you and if you resist them, they’ll come with guns and they’ll put you in jail.” This coercive backing, protected by military superpower status, is what makes the dollar “the best currency in the world” to foreign creditors.

Thiel identifies a fundamental contradiction at the heart of America’s debt crisis: Americans believe “we’re never gonna pay [the debt] off” and we’ll just “keep borrowing more forever,” while foreigners expect to get repaid in valuable dollars backed by military might. These conflicting expectations cannot both be true. The unspoken question becomes whether military power will ultimately protect the Federal Reserve’s ability to print money — or whether foreign creditors might have the military force to eventually demand “real money” instead of printed dollars. As Thiel notes, this critical tension “is never really articulated” in public discourse.
